newsitem.title: INDIA: Experts hunt for clues to India air disaster.
newsitem.headline: Experts hunt for clues to India air disaster.

text.p: Indian aviation experts were baffled on Wednesday by the cause of world's worst mid-air collision but said a misunderstanding on heights and language problems could have been factors behind the tragedy.
S. S. Sidhu, a former secretary general of the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), said it would be difficult at this stage to pin-point the cause of the crash.
"Either it could be error on the part of the air traffic control or human error," he told Reuters.
Brij Bharadwaj, an independent aviation expert, said: "The most likely cause could be a misunderstanding about the height of the two aircraft."

Some 350 people were believed killed when a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet taking off from New Delhi's Indira Gandhi International airport and an incoming Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 collided. The exact death toll in the crash will not be known until the official manifests are officially released.
It was India's worst aviation disaster.
Wreckage and burning bodies, some recognisable as women and children, were spread over six km (four miles) of fields near Charkhi Dadri village, 80 km (50 miles) southwest of New Delhi.

Sidhu said many pilots of aircraft of CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) countries had faced language problems, even before the break-up of the Soviet Union. Most of these pilots had earlier flown only in the Soviet Union.
"Overall, internationally speaking, 75 percent of the cause of air accidents is human error. Mechanical or systems failures are only 25 percent," Sidhu told Reuters.
Bharadwaj said the pilots of both aircraft had been instructed to fly at a certain height. "At the time when they were given the instructions, it is crucial at what height they were flying."
He also said the tragedy could have been due to the language barrier, thus causing a misunderstanding between air traffic controllers and the Kazakh pilot.
H.S. Khola, the director general of civil aviation (DGCA), told reporters late on Tuesday the Saudi flight had been cleared to climb to flight level of 14,000 feet (4,308 metres).
The Kazakh aircraft was instructed to descend to 15,000 feet (4,615 metres) by air traffic control.
Sidhu said the height separation conformed with safety standards laid down by the Montreal-based ICAO.
DGCA officials said the immediate cause of the accident would be known only after the black boxes of both aircraft had been retrieved.
Experts said there was only one course for arrival and departure routes at Delhi airport.

One expert, who asked not to be identified, said the disaster might have been averted if transponders had been installed at the airport, as suggested by the Indian Commercial Pilots Association (ICPA).
"If transponders were installed, the ground controllers would have visually seen the two airplanes converging at the same altitude and could have sounded the alarm," he said.
The ICPA regional president, V.K. Bhalla, said in a letter to the civil aviation ministry last year that navigation and communication systems in India were not up to international standards.
The ICPA had demanded installation of transponders at major Indian airports. It said that since October, 1994, three potential mid-air collision had been averted over India.
